overview: This record covers Lithuania’s interwar state and the wartime years included by the atlas. Independence was proclaimed in 1918, before the first 1920 snapshot. New institutions, modern buildings and broadcasting developed, but democracy was overthrown in 1926 and independence was lost to Soviet occupation in 1940.

periods.title: Independence and parliamentary government
periods.summary: The declaration of 1918 preceded the atlas’s first snapshot.

periods.title: Authoritarian rule and modernization
periods.summary: The military coup interrupted democracy while Kaunas continued developing as provisional capital.

periods.title: Successive occupations
periods.summary: Soviet occupation was followed by Nazi occupation and the Holocaust, then renewed Soviet rule.

sections.title: Independence and who had a voice

items.text: The Council of Lithuania signed the independence act on 16 February 1918 in a rented Vilnius apartment. The building also housed a well-known pastry shop. A moment of national politics occurred amid ordinary commercial and residential life.

Atstatanti nepriklausomą means “restoring an independent…” These Lithuanian words come from the 1918 declaration, as quoted by the National Museum. The short excerpt belongs to a political document and uses Latin letters with Lithuanian diacritics.

The following day, women protested in Kaunas because none had been included in the Council that declared independence. The episode shows disagreement about whose participation counted, even during a celebrated founding moment.

Armed officers interrupted parliament during the December 1926 coup. Antanas Smetona became president, and the Third Seimas was dissolved in April 1927. Interwar statehood must therefore be distinguished from uninterrupted democratic rule.

sections.title: Building a capital and connecting homes

items.text: Kaunas served as provisional capital from 1919 to 1939. Public buildings and homes expanded within an inherited street plan. Modernization involved adapting an existing town, rather than clearing a blank space and beginning again.

The New Town developed as an administrative centre, while Green Hill followed a garden-suburb plan from 1923. Their different streets and building patterns preserve contrasting ideas about where people should work, live and spend time outdoors.

Lithuanian radio began broadcasting from Kaunas on 12 June 1926. Hearing information and performances at home introduced a new daily rhythm. Access still depended on having or sharing a receiver; a national broadcast was not proof that every family listened.

The museum preserves a Philips Deutschland 456A radio made in 1936 to 1937. A receiver was both equipment and furniture. Its case and controls help make early broadcasting a household experience, rather than just a date in a communications timeline.

sections.title: Families, music and lives across borders

items.text: The Hofmekler family moved from Vilnius to Kaunas in 1920. Several family members played different instruments, and Michelis helped organize early radio concerts. Their work documents a Jewish contribution to the city’s musical life through named people and surviving records.

The National Museum estimates that about 104,000 people left Lithuania between 1918 and 1940, many heading to South America. An independent state could still have families separated by work and migration. Departure did not necessarily end their connections.

Migrants also sent money and parcels home. The museum records substantial support from Lithuanian Americans during the first independence decade. Family networks crossed oceans and contributed to the resources available within the new state.

The signatories’ museum preserves objects such as Aleksandras Stulginskis’s watch, carried through public service and later deportation. Personal possessions can connect official history with a life’s changes, but a famous person’s object is not a typical household sample.

Soviet occupation in 1940 ended independent government. Nazi occupation followed in 1941, bringing the Holocaust to Lithuania; renewed Soviet rule followed in 1944. These were violent changes affecting real communities, not a peaceful sequence of map colours.

ending.text: The Soviet Union occupied Lithuania in June 1940 and annexed it that summer. Nazi occupation and the Holocaust followed, then renewed Soviet rule. The atlas extends this label to 1945, but the independent interwar government had already ended. Lithuania’s people continued through persecution, resistance, exile and later restoration.
